title: TransXplainRRG: A Radiologist-Evaluated LVLM for Chest Radiograph Report Generation
authors: Chayan Mondal, Duc-Son Pham, Tele Tan, Ashu Gupta, Vincent T. Y. Tiong, Shreya Ghosh
abstract: Recent advancements in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLM) enhance X-ray report generation, but often neglect clinical context, overlook workflow integration, and lack explainability, which hinders clinical adoption due to interpretability and reliability concerns. This paper addresses the dual challenges of performance and expert explainability in automated X-ray report generation for clinical AI applications. Our proposed approach, TransXplainRRG, utilises an off-the-shelf Swin Transformer model along with a transformer-based text encoder that incorporates patient medical history to generate a radiology report. Further, we explore an expert-guided `inside-out' approach and extract only abnormal findings for radiology report refinement. Thus, this study bridges the gap between high-performance automation and interpretability critical for clinical practice by combining state-of-the-art transformer-based vision encoders, text encoders, and LLMs. TransXplainRRG is trained and tested on the large-scale MIMIC-CXR dataset and further evaluated on the unseen IU X-Ray dataset to demonstrate its generalizability and robustness. We employed the GREEN metric as a complementary measure of clinical consistency, achieving scores of 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray, both higher than those achieved by MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation setting. It also performed competitively across standard evaluation metrics, frequently matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we introduce qualitative evaluation metrics developed from radiologists' viewpoints and conduct a preliminary radiologist evaluation on 100 generated reports to assess their clinical relevance. Quantitative and qualitative analyses further demonstrate the potential of our TransXplainRRG framework for reliable and explainable radiology report generation.

infographic.key_insight: TransXplainRRG combines chest X-rays and patient history to generate reports, with expert-guided refinement aimed at improving clinical consistency and explainability.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support radiology reporting workflows, but its suitability for routine clinical use remains unestablished.
method: Encode chest X-rays with a Swin Transformer and patient history with a transformer-based text encoder.
Use an expert-guided “inside-out” approach and extract abnormal findings to refine reports.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained and tested on MIMIC-CXR and evaluated on unseen IU X-Ray data, it achieved GREEN scores of 0.327 and 0.605, respectively—above MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation setting—with preliminary radiologist review of 100 generated reports.
infographic.watch_item: Preliminary review of 100 reports does not establish clinical safety or workflow benefit; prospective validation is still needed.
infographic.paper_title: TransXplainRRG: A Radiologist-Evaluated LVLM for Chest Radiograph Report Generation

title: Curiosity-0826-4B: Generative Medical Event Sequence Modeling Across Pediatric and Adult Populations
authors: Mani Nagarathnam, Luke Benham, Paul Blazek, John Cashy, Kevin Chung, John Muenning
abstract: We introduce Curiosity-0826-4B, an updated version of the generative medical event foundation model trained on Epic Cosmos that simulates patient timelines to produce zero-shot clinical predictions. Curiosity-0826-4B incorporates a broader patient population and richer clinical event representations, while generally matching or exceeding Curiosity-0226-1B, the largest model in the previous Curiosity-0226 series, on evaluated tasks supported by both models. Laboratory value prediction improved, with MAE 18--46% lower than that of Curiosity-0226-1B. We evaluated prediction of disease events across pediatric cohorts aged 2--17 years. AUROCs for new asthma diagnosis (0.742--0.785) and asthma exacerbation (0.829--0.852) were comparable to those in the adult reference cohort, while AUROCs for sickle cell crisis (0.820--0.847) were lower than in adults (0.915). Explicit representation of documented death enabled new mortality prediction tasks among adults across hospice, inpatient, and ambulatory settings (AUROC 0.821--0.942). Scaling-law analysis guided compute-optimal initial pretraining followed by continued pretraining with context extension. The resulting Curiosity-0826-4B model has more parameters (4.3B versus 1B) and a longer context window (16K versus 8K). It processes 56% fewer training tokens and requires 2.2 times the training floating point operations (FLOPs) compared with its predecessor. By extending a common zero-shot prediction strategy to pediatric patients and additional outcomes, Curiosity-0826-4B broadens opportunities to develop clinical and operational applications without training separate task-specific models. Further validation should assess local calibration, performance across patient subgroups and event frequencies, timeline completion rates, and generalization to new settings, alongside prospective evaluation of clinical and operational utility.

infographic.key_insight: Curiosity-0826-4B broadens zero-shot medical event prediction to pediatric populations and adult mortality, while reducing laboratory prediction error versus its predecessor.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A shared model could support multiple clinical and operational prediction tasks without separate task-specific training, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Trained on Epic Cosmos to simulate patient timelines and predict future events.
Expanded patient coverage and clinical event representations, including documented death.
Used scaling-law-guided pretraining and context extension to reach 4.3B parameters and a 16K context window.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations reported 18–46% lower laboratory MAE than Curiosity-0226-1B, pediatric disease-event AUROCs of 0.742–0.852, and adult mortality AUROCs of 0.821–0.942.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires validation of local calibration, subgroup performance, generalization to new settings, and prospective clinical utility.

title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks
authors: Ashvin Gupta, Brendan Delaney, Alessandra Russo
abstract: Structured Electronic Health Records (EHR) models typically treat each clinical concept as a dataset-specific token, discarding the natural-language semantics associated with the event. As a result, relationships between concepts must largely be learned from EHR co-occurrence, without directly exploiting any prior semantic knowledge. We investigate how pretrained causal language models can be adapted for longitudinal EHR prediction by developing tEHR. Here, we represent events with their natural language description and use this text stream to apply EHR-adaptive continued pretraining, followed by task-specific discriminative fine-tuning using LoRA, utilising the LLM as a longitudinal patient-encoder. We evaluate this approach across four prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset and pancreatic cancer prediction on the CPRD dataset at 1 to 12 month horizons, with tEHR using the Mistral-7B-v0.3 backbone achieving the strongest overall performance. Ablations show that performance declines when clinical descriptions are removed or misaligned, when numerical values are omitted, and when either stage of adaptation is removed, while explicit elapsed-time descriptions provide little additional benefit. Analysis of the learned patient representations further reveals clinically coherent structure associated with distinct patterns of disease risk and clinical history.

infographic.key_insight: tEHR uses pretrained language semantics to encode longitudinal health records, with clinical descriptions and numerical values contributing to prediction performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support EHR-based risk prediction, but the abstract does not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Represent structured EHR events using natural-language descriptions.
Continue pretraining a causal language model on longitudinal EHR text.
Use LoRA for task-specific discriminative fine-tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered four MIMIC-IV prediction tasks and CPRD pancreatic cancer prediction at 1–12-month horizons; Mistral-7B-v0.3 achieved the strongest overall performance among the tested tEHR backbones.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical performance estimates or prospective clinical evaluation, limiting assessment of clinical utility.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating Pretrained Language Semantics for Structured EHR Prediction Tasks

title: Fine-Tuned Small Language Model for Synthetic Clinical Data Generation and Predictive Healthcare Analytics
authors: Mihnea Sebastian Burlacu, Ionut Anghel, Tudor Cioara
abstract: The reduced availability of medical datasets represents an important challenge in the development of predictive models for remote healthcare solutions, especially when the available data are imbalanced or difficult to extend through traditional methods. Small Language Models (SLMs) have become a promising alternative to Large Language Models (LLMs) for addressing these limitations due to their lower computational requirements and adaptability to specialized tasks. However, their performance remains highly dependent on the quality and representativeness of the available training data. In this paper, we propose a method for clinical data augmentation based on a fine-tuned Microsoft Phi-2 model that is used to generate synthetic instances, with the purpose of improving deep learning-based model for predicting remotely monitored vital signs. The Phi-2 model was adapted to the medical domain through supervised fine-tuning on the MedQuad dataset, through a Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA)-based method and by applying few-shot prompting techniques. The resulting model was used afterwards in the augmentation of a small-sized dataset, composed of vital sign values and labels associated with pathological and physiological states. The experimental results demonstrate that fine-tuned SLMs improved the performance on medical domain, achieving higher scores for both lexical (ROUGE) and semantic (BERTScore) evaluation metrics compared to the pretrained model. Moreover, the fine-tuned SLM is effective for generating structured synthetic clinical data. When used for data augmentation, the generated dataset improved the performance of a LSTM predictive model, increasing the classification accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7% and showing consistent improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score.

infographic.key_insight: Synthetic clinical data generated by a fine-tuned Phi-2 model improved an LSTM classifier’s reported accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7%.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support predictive modeling for remotely monitored vital signs when labeled clinical datasets are small or imbalanced.
method: Adapted Microsoft Phi-2 to medical content using MedQuad and supervised QLoRA fine-tuning.
Used few-shot prompting to generate structured synthetic vital-sign records and physiological/pathological labels.
Augmented a small dataset to train an LSTM predictive model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved ROUGE and BERTScore versus pretrained Phi-2, alongside higher LSTM accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score after augmentation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report dataset size or external validation, leaving generalizability to real-world patient populations uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Fine-Tuned Small Language Model for Synthetic Clinical Data Generation and Predictive Healthcare Analytics

title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging
authors: Chenhui Zhao, Akshay Rao, Akhil Kondepudi, Yiwei Lyu, Xinhai Hou, Rikhil Seshadri
abstract: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Neuro-VL is a specialized vision-language model that interprets complete neuroimaging examinations and discusses findings in natural language.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Its capabilities could support radiology reporting and longitudinal disease assessment, but the abstract does not establish improved patient outcomes.
method: Trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care.
Interprets examinations, describes abnormalities and generates radiology reports.
Compares serial examinations and responds to questions about findings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed general-purpose and specialized medical models on reported imaging tasks and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective clinical validation is needed to establish safety and reliability before routine deployment.
infographic.paper_title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging

title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control
authors: Bowen Wang, Osvaldo Simeone
abstract: Online conformal risk control (OCRC) enables reliable uncertainty quantification in machine learning by converting model outputs into prediction sets with long-term risk guarantees. These guarantees, however, hinge on the assumption that the loss of each round is revealed immediately and losslessly. In practice, feedback may be delayed, and limited resources may prevent tracking all pending predictions, causing some feedback to be lost. To address this challenge, we develop capacity-aware OCRC (CA-OCRC), a framework that jointly determines how to allocate limited tracking feedback capacity and how to construct prediction sets. CA-OCRC is based on a randomized tracking policy that samples a proxy delay to decide whether, and for how long, feedback for the current round is tracked. CA-OCRC updates the prediction sets via inverse probability weighting, compensating for the possibility of feedback lost due to delays and limited tracking capacity. We analyze risk bounds for both arbitrary and stochastic delays, revealing a trade-off between receiving more feedback and avoiding capacity saturation. Building on these bounds, we optimize the proxy delay distribution, showing scaling laws for the tracking capacity that ensure the same long-term risk as OCRC with unlimited feedback. Experiments on medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications show the effectiveness of CA-OCRC as compared to existing OCRC mechanisms.

infographic.key_insight: Capacity-aware online conformal risk control (CA-OCRC) adapts prediction sets when delayed feedback and limited tracking capacity would otherwise undermine long-term risk guarantees.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For medical imaging AI, this approach could support uncertainty quantification when outcome feedback arrives late and not every prediction can be tracked.
method: Randomly samples a proxy delay to decide whether and how long to track each prediction.
Uses inverse probability weighting to account for feedback lost through delays or capacity limits.
Optimizes tracking policies using risk bounds that balance feedback collection against capacity saturation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical risk bounds and experiments spanning medical imaging, natural language processing, computer vision, and wireless communications, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Long-term risk guarantees do not establish per-patient safety; clinical deployment would require validation under local feedback delays and tracking constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Capacity-Constrained Delayed Feedback for Online Conformal Risk Control

title: Redefining Synovial Pathotypes in Psoriatic Arthritis through Multi-Modal Histology and Machine Learning (The PSYNOVIUM Study)
authors: Hum, R. M.; Christofi, M.; Smith, S. L.; Tan, Y.; Shukla, R.; Marshall, L. M.; Smith, M.; Williams, A.; Orozco, G.; Viatte, S.; Buch, M.; Barton, A.; Ho, P.; Martin, P.
abstract: BackgroundSynovial inflammation in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) lacks a validated histological classification framework. Current approaches apply rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovial pathotypes to PsA, which overlooks immunobiological differences between the diseases and limits the predictive power of tissue stratification. We aimed to define data-driven, PsA-specific synovial pathotypes to facilitate tissue-driven precision medicine. MethodsIn this cross-sectional study, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were obtained from 61 patients with PsA (n=22), seropositive RA (n=23), seronegative RA (n=10), and other inflammatory arthritides (n=6). Sections underwent multi-modal staining, including H&E, picrosirius red, and immunohisto-chemistry for CD3, CD20, CD68, CD138, and CD31. Whole-slide digital image analysis and automated pixel classifiers quantified cellular and stromal metrics. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified intrinsic PsA pathotypes, which were correlated with clinical disease activity, radiographic osteoarthritis (OA), and longitudinal treatment responses. FindingsWhile a subset of PsA patients shared an inflammatory signature with seropositive RA, unsupervised clustering of the PsA cohort revealed three distinct, novel pathotypes: Dense Myeloid (macrophage-driven), Fibro-Stromal (fibrosis and pauci-immune), and Angio-Lymphoid (hypervascular with significant CD138+ plasma cell infiltration). Pathotypes were independent of treatment and concurrent radiographic knee OA. The Fibro-Stromal pathotype correlated with significantly higher cutaneous psoriasis severity. Longitudinally, patients with the Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited a trend toward lower treatment response (44%) following standard interventions (methotrexate or TNF inhibitors) compared to the Dense Myeloid (50%) and Angio-Lymphoid (80%) pathotypes. InterpretationWe present the first computationally derived synovial pathotypes specific to PsA, revealing distinct plasma cell and fibrotic architectures not captured by RA-centric models. To enable clinical translation, we distilled these findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red) designed for routine histopathology workflows, providing a staging ground for biomarker-stratified clinical trials in PsA. FundingFunding from the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre: Manchester, Arthritis UK, the Wellcome Trust, Brit-PACT, the National Psoriasis Foundation, and the Medical Research Council. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSThe potential clinical utility of tissue-based patient stratification is well established in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), where baseline synovial pathotypes (lympho-myeloid, diffuse-myeloid, and pauciimmune) have guided targeted biologic therapy in landmark precision medicine trials. However, psoriatic arthritis (PsA) exhibits a fundamentally distinct synovial microenvironment, characterised by unique vascular architecture, altered stromal fibroblast phenotypes, and distinct immune infiltrates intertwined with the IL-23/IL-17 cytokine axis. Consequently, attempting to classify PsA synovial tissue using established RA-derived scoring systems risks misrepresenting intrinsic disease biology. There is currently no validated, disease-specific histological classification system for PsA, which forces therapeutic decision-making to rely on an empirical, trial-and-error approach rather than underlying target tissue pathobiology. Added value of this studyTo our knowledge, this is the first study to define data-driven, computationally derived synovial pathotypes entirely specific to PsA. By leveraging multi-modal digital pathology and unsupervised machine learning, we deconstructed the PsA synovium into three biologically distinct pathotypes: Dense Myeloid, Fibro-Stromal, and Angio-Lymphoid. We demonstrated that the highly inflammatory PsA microenvironment is distinctly driven by CD138+ plasma cells rather than the CD20+ B cells typically observed in RA. Furthermore, we identified a striking tissue-level divergence: patients with the highly fibrotic, pauci-immune Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited the most severe cutaneous psoriasis and demonstrated a trend toward higher failure rates on standard therapies, independent of concurrent osteoarthritis. Crucially, we translated these high-dimensional computational findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (incorporating CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red). Implications of all the available evidenceThis study establishes that PsA synovial pathology requires a dedicated, disease-specific classification framework. The proposed diagnostic decision tree can be integrated into routine clinical histopathology workflows without the immediate need for advanced spatial or single-cell transcriptomics. Furthermore, the correlation between the Fibro-Stromal pathotype, severe skin disease, and poor joint response to standard therapies provides a biological rationale for stratifying this specific subgroup towards early IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor intervention alongside conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. Ultimately, these novel PsA pathotypes provide the vital staging ground required to design and execute biomarker-stratified, tissue-driven clinical trials, paving the way for precision medicine in PsA.

infographic.key_insight: Computational analysis identified three PsA-specific synovial pathotypes: Dense Myeloid, Fibro-Stromal, and Angio-Lymphoid.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These tissue patterns could support future patient stratification, but their ability to guide treatment remains unvalidated.
method: Ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies from 61 patients, including 22 with PsA.
Multi-modal staining, whole-slide image analysis, and automated pixel classifiers quantified cellular and stromal features.
Unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified PsA pathotypes, which were compared with clinical features and treatment responses.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the 22-patient PsA cohort, reported treatment response rates were 44% for Fibro-Stromal, 50% for Dense Myeloid, and 80% for Angio-Lymphoid—a descriptive trend rather than established predictive performance.
infographic.watch_item: The small PsA cohort and lack of reported external validation limit confidence in the proposed four-marker decision tree.
infographic.paper_title: Redefining Synovial Pathotypes in Psoriatic Arthritis through Multi-Modal Histology and Machine Learning (The PSYNOVIUM Study)

title: KQML-Liver: Interpretable Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Liver Disease Classification
authors: Nhat-Long Nguyen, Viet-Loi Dinh, Trong-Nghia Pham
abstract: Liver disease remains a major global health concern, highlighting the need for reliable and accessible early detection methods. Although recent advances in machine learning, deep learning and quantum machine learning (QML) have introduced promising diagnostic tools, many approaches suffer from limited interpretability and inflated performance caused by data leakage or overly simplistic evaluation protocols. These constraints reduce their reliability in real-world clinical practice. This paper proposes KQML-Liver, a hybrid framework that integrates QML with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to enhance predictive performance and interpretability. The architecture combines parameterized quantum circuits for expressive feature representation with KAN-based functional mappings that capture nonlinear relationships in an interpretable manner. Evaluated on the Indian Liver Patient Dataset (ILPD) under a rigorous preprocessing protocol preventing data leakage, the proposed model achieves 82% classification accuracy and 100% recall, detecting all positive cases, outperforming existing baselines while providing improved transparency in clinical predictions. These results suggest that hybrid KAN-quantum architectures offer a promising direction for interpretable AI-assisted medical diagnosis.

infographic.key_insight: KQML-Liver combines quantum machine learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, reporting 82% accuracy and 100% recall for liver disease classification.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more interpretable liver disease detection, but clinical usefulness remains unproven.
method: Parameterized quantum circuits represent input features.
Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks model nonlinear relationships.
Leakage-prevention preprocessing supports evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the Indian Liver Patient Dataset, the authors report 82% accuracy and 100% recall, outperforming evaluated baselines under a protocol designed to prevent data leakage.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no external validation or specificity, leaving generalizability and false-positive burden uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: KQML-Liver: Interpretable Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Liver Disease Classification

title: Constructing and Validating Memorisation Audits for EHR Foundation Models
authors: Inigo Stibbe, Joshua Placidi, Padmanabhan Ramnarayan, A. Aldo Faisal
abstract: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models may disclose training information at inference, yet clinical predictability makes patient-specific memorisation difficult to distinguish from generalisation. We evaluate fixed-window token reconstruction, sensitive-attribute disclosure, and random patient-level canaries in GPT-2-style models trained on MIMIC-IV, across early, best-validation, and final checkpoints. Reconstruction improves with additional context, but training--held-out differences remain small. Trajectory-unique prompts containing limited clinical information produce no excess sensitive disclosure for training patients. In a matched model with random binary patient-level canaries, training-patient label-recovery AUROC increases from 0.512 to 0.549 while held-out recovery remains at chance. An overfit 1,000-patient positive control achieves near-perfect recovery, confirming sensitivity to strong memorisation. These results reveal weak cohort-level memorisation but no reliable patient-level disclosure under the evaluated attacks. They motivate clinically grounded inference-time audits that can detect patient-specific memorisation in existing models without retraining with canaries.

infographic.key_insight: EHR foundation models showed weak cohort-level memorisation but no reliable patient-level disclosure under the evaluated attacks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Privacy audits must distinguish patient-specific memorisation from predictable clinical patterns when assessing EHR model disclosure risks.
method: Evaluated GPT-2-style models trained on MIMIC-IV at early, best-validation, and final checkpoints.
Tested fixed-window token reconstruction, sensitive-attribute disclosure, and random patient-level canary recovery.
Used an overfit 1,000-patient model as a positive control for strong memorisation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training-patient canary recovery AUROC rose from 0.512 to 0.549 while held-out recovery stayed at chance; the overfit positive control achieved near-perfect recovery.
infographic.watch_item: These findings do not establish privacy safety beyond the evaluated models, prompts, and attacks.
infographic.paper_title: Constructing and Validating Memorisation Audits for EHR Foundation Models

title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Federico Ravenda, Mirko Cesarini, Daniele Montagnani, Volodymyr Karpenko, Antonietta Mira, Andrea Raballo
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve expert-level diagnostic accuracy in static evaluations, where the model receives a curated vignette or case report that already condenses the diagnostically relevant findings. Such evaluations measure inference over already selected evidence; the evaluations do not account for the inquiry used to obtain it. In clinical practice, however, diagnosis is an iterative process of inquiry. Clinicians take the patient's history, or anamnesis (Hx), through targeted questioning, examine the patient, and request and interpret tests, progressively narrowing the differential until they reach a final diagnosis (Dx). We introduce Hx2Dx ARENA, an interactive benchmark of 1'000 clinical cases from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM). Each case is a simulated encounter that proceeds from initial presentation through history taking and physical examination to diagnostic workup. We evaluate open- and closed-source LLMs under multiple configurations. Performance varies considerably across models in the interactive setting, and every model loses diagnostic accuracy relative to the static setting, where the full case is presented upfront. The ability to ask the right questions accounts for much of both the gap between models and the loss of accuracy: diagnosis improves as questions become more targeted and build a more complete clinical picture. LLMs thus reason well once the relevant data are available but remain limited in hypothesis-driven information gathering, in knowing what to ask in order to know. Closing this gap is a prerequisite for their safe integration into real-world diagnostic workflows.

infographic.key_insight: LLMs lose diagnostic accuracy when they must gather clinical information interactively rather than receive a complete case upfront.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating how models obtain relevant information—not just interpret it—is important before considering their use in diagnostic workflows.
method: Introduced Hx2Dx ARENA using 1,000 NEJM clinical cases.
Simulated encounters spanning history taking, physical examination, and diagnostic workup.
Evaluated open- and closed-source LLMs across configurations and compared interactive with static performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Every evaluated model performed worse interactively than with the full case provided upfront; more targeted questioning was associated with better diagnostic performance.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from simulated encounters and do not establish safety or effectiveness in real-world patient care.
infographic.paper_title: Hx2Dx: From Anamnesis to Diagnosis - A Multimodal Arena for Conversational Clinical Reasoning in LLMs

title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen
authors: Richard J. Young, Alice M. Matthews
abstract: Racial and ethnic minority patients receive less pain treatment than non-Hispanic White patients, and large language models (LLMs) used as medical AI could reproduce that bias. Prior audits tested a few proprietary models, stated race explicitly and rarely measured the models' own response instability. In exploratory, non-preregistered analyses, Study 1 had four open-weight LLMs assess six acute-pain vignettes in every combination of four races and two sexes, with identity stated or cued only by a name (two names per group), comparing each identity with a White male reference on the same case and sampling seed. In Study 2, 24 configurations of 17 models, including OpenAI's GPT-4.1 mini and gpt-oss, Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5, Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash, Meta's Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen, with reasoning on and off and at two precisions, answered the same vignettes and the 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases. In this single-prompt, JSON-constrained task, no difference survived correction in Study 1, none of 1,386 comparisons survived the false discovery rate in Study 2, and every pain-severity difference was equivalent to zero within one point on a 0-10 scale (within a quarter point for 237 of 238 Q-Pain comparisons). Opioid decisions were bounded less precisely (Study 1 could not exclude differences of about 20 percentage points), so they show no detected difference, not proof of none. The few differences surviving correction within a model favoured Black patients. Models differed far more from one another and across their own settings than between patients (the reference patient received the high opioid dose in 6% to 93% of responses), although serving software, provider and prompt format also differed. Fairness audits of clinical AI should use several names per group, pair comparisons on the seed, report the noise floor and test each deployed configuration.

infographic.key_insight: This audit found no racial or sex differences surviving study-wide correction, while pain-management recommendations varied substantially across models and settings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Clinical AI fairness evaluations should test each deployed configuration, because model and setting choices may affect recommendations more than patient identity in these tasks.
method: Study 1 tested four open-weight models on six acute-pain vignettes, varying race and sex through explicit labels or names.
Identity comparisons were paired to a White male reference using the same case and sampling seed.
Study 2 evaluated 24 configurations of 17 models on the same vignettes and 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: None of 1,386 Study 2 comparisons survived false-discovery-rate correction; all pain-severity differences met equivalence bounds of ±1 point on a 0–10 scale.
infographic.watch_item: These exploratory, single-prompt findings do not establish absence of bias: opioid estimates were less precise, with Study 1 unable to exclude differences of about 20 percentage points.
infographic.paper_title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen

title: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation: Differentiable Length Control for Concise Clinical Reasoning in Smaller Language Models
authors: Tanzeel Abbas, Ahmad Kamran Malik, Nafees Qamar, Sana Liaqat
abstract: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.

infographic.key_insight: PECA reduced mean response length by 72.8% while increasing multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0% in a 1.7-billion-parameter language model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Shorter medical responses could reduce reading burden in time-constrained workflows, but clinical usefulness and safety remain unestablished.
method: Adds a differentiable conciseness term to QLoRA supervised fine-tuning.
Encourages end-of-sequence generation after a token budget is exceeded.
Requires no preference data or auxiliary model and trains on a single commodity GPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports fine-tuning on medical-o1-reasoning-SFT and multiple-choice diagnostic evaluation, with a conciseness-strength sweep mapping accuracy–length trade-offs.
infographic.watch_item: Results from one model and multiple-choice evaluation do not establish whether shorter responses preserve clinically important details in real-world use.
infographic.paper_title: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation: Differentiable Length Control for Concise Clinical Reasoning in Smaller Language Models

title: The BRIDGE dataset: paired brightfield whole-slide images of prostate core-needle biopsies in paraffin, after deparaffinization and H&E staining
authors: Julia A. Mielcarz, Justyna Durślewicz, Marek Zdrenka, Ahmad Abbadi, Martin Eklund, Mateusz Matusiak
abstract: Computational approaches are increasingly being explored to streamline histopathology workflows, including label-free methods that aim to reduce reliance on chemical staining. Among these, deep learning-based label-free virtual staining uses images of unstained tissue to computationally generate stained images. Despite growing interest, model development and validation remain constrained by the scarcity of paired, clinically annotated whole-slide imaging datasets. We present BRIDGE, a dataset of prostate core-needle biopsies collected at the Prof. Franciszek Lukaszczyk Oncology Centre in Bydgoszcz, Poland. The dataset comprises 869 glass slides from 169 patients, each digitized sequentially after sectioning, deparaffinization, and hematoxylin and eosin staining, yielding in total 2607 whole-slide images. The dataset supports the development and external validation of label-free virtual staining, virtual unstaining, image-registration and segmentation methods. Each slide is accompanied by a Gleason score, enabling downstream analyses of cancer classification and grading concordance. The stained images can be used independently for color normalization and cross-scanner robustness studies. All images are de-identified, distributed in their native scanner format and will be available through the BioImage Archive.

infographic.key_insight: BRIDGE pairs prostate biopsy whole-slide images across three preparation stages to support research on AI-based virtual staining and related imaging methods.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Gleason annotations enable research on whether virtual staining preserves information relevant to prostate cancer classification and grading.
method: Collect 869 prostate biopsy slides from 169 patients at one oncology centre in Poland.
Digitize each slide in paraffin, after deparaffinization, and after H&E staining.
Provide de-identified images in native scanner format with slide-level Gleason scores.
infographic.evidence_signal: The dataset contains 2,607 whole-slide images; the abstract reports no model performance or clinical validation results.
infographic.watch_item: Single-centre sourcing may limit generalizability, requiring validation across institutions and imaging workflows.
infographic.paper_title: The BRIDGE dataset: paired brightfield whole-slide images of prostate core-needle biopsies in paraffin, after deparaffinization and H&E staining

title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
authors: Yihan Hank Tang, Peng Yang, Jiayi Xin, Tianqi Shang, Xuyang Chen, Ying Yuan
abstract: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.

infographic.key_insight: TrialDesignBench reveals gaps between frontier LLMs and expert-validated statistical designs for early-phase oncology trials.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark supports research toward AI-assisted dose-finding trial design aligned with contemporary FDA initiatives, including Project Optimus.
method: Compile 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials.
Pair each trial with an expert-validated reference design using a formalized expert process.
Evaluate five frontier LLMs and probe performance gaps through ablation experiments.
infographic.evidence_signal: None of the five LLMs matched the reference standard; supplying latent design determinants and structured decision-tree reasoning improved class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22 and 0.24, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance does not establish readiness for real-world trial design, particularly when critical design determinants are unrecorded.
infographic.paper_title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge

title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
authors: Mingchen Li, Yongkang Xiao, Rumeng Li, Rui Zhang, Hong Yu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in biomedical applications, while agentic memory systems have emerged as a promising approach to preserving and utilizing information across tasks and interactions. However, a fundamental question remains: how effectively and reliably do these systems retain, retrieve, update, and utilize biomedical information? In this study, we systematically investigate agentic memory in the biomedical domain, focusing on task effectiveness, retrieval quality, information fidelity, and long-term robustness. We evaluate five memory approaches across four LLMs in three representative settings: biomedical knowledge reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory. Our analyses reveal how memory construction, evidence relevance, and conversational history shape downstream biomedical performance, highlighting the distinct challenges of retrieving relevant information, preserving its fidelity, and effectively utilizing it for reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce Hybrid Memory Retrieval and Utilization (HMRU), a training-free framework that jointly enhances evidence accessibility and task-aware utilization to improve biomedical reasoning and long-term conversational memory. HMRU achieves an average relative improvement of 8.6% across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks. It further reduces conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closes 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference. Our findings provide a systematic characterization of biomedical agentic memory and practical insights into developing more effective and reliable memory-augmented LLM systems.

infographic.key_insight: BioMem introduces HMRU, a training-free memory framework reporting an average 8.6% relative improvement across biomedical question-answering and conversational memory benchmarks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More reliable memory could help biomedical LLM agents use relevant prior information, but these results do not establish clinical safety or patient benefit.
method: Evaluated five memory approaches across four LLMs.
Tested biomedical reasoning, clinical prediction, and long-term conversational memory.
Developed HMRU to improve evidence accessibility and task-aware use.
infographic.evidence_signal: HMRU reduced conversational answer errors by 24.9% and closed 48.0% of the performance gap to full-context inference, with additional gains in selected clinical prediction tasks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify dataset sizes or clinical deployment validation; retrieval relevance and information fidelity remain important implementation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents

title: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model
authors: Guoan Wang, Feng Liu
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are pretrained on thousands of hours of recordings, yet their frozen features transfer poorly to downstream tasks, and this transfer does not consistently improve with larger models or more pretraining data. We show that a vision foundation model that has never seen EEG is a stronger frozen EEG encoder than these specialized models, once the signals are rendered as images that a vision transformer can read. Our method, SeeEEG, keeps the vision backbone frozen and learns only how EEG is displayed to it. Each channel occupies a dedicated row of patches and is drawn either as a waveform at a fixed gain or as a scalogram whose frequency range spans the patch height, so that task-relevant patterns fall within individual tokens. The montage, filtering, and contrast parameters of this display are initialized from a standard clinical montage and optimized with the task loss through the frozen backbone, which amounts to at most 1,113 trainable parameters per view. We compare SeeEEG with seven EEG foundation models on eight clinical, sleep, affective, and brain-computer interface datasets, with every encoder frozen and paired with identical readout heads. With a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B, SeeEEG outperforms every EEG foundation model in balanced accuracy on all eight datasets and reaches a mean rank of 1.3 in Cohen kappa or AUROC, compared with 2.9 for the strongest baseline, REVE. The learned displays transfer without further optimization to the video encoder V-JEPA 2.1, which outperforms every EEG foundation model on both metrics on six of the eight datasets. Replacing DINOv3 with a randomly initialized ViT-B lowers the score by 15.2 points on average, so the ability to read rendered EEG comes from visual pretraining.

infographic.key_insight: SeeEEG turns EEG signals into images, enabling a frozen vision foundation model to outperform specialized frozen EEG encoders across eight datasets.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support EEG analysis across clinical and sleep-related tasks, but these benchmarks do not establish readiness for clinical use.
method: Render each EEG channel as a waveform or scalogram in a dedicated row of image patches.
Optimize montage, filtering, and contrast through a frozen vision backbone using at most 1,113 trainable display parameters per view.
Compare frozen encoders using identical readout heads.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against seven EEG foundation models on eight datasets, SeeEEG with DINOv3 ViT-B achieved higher balanced accuracy than every comparator on all eight; random initialization reduced scores by 15.2 points on average.
infographic.watch_item: The results concern frozen-encoder benchmarks; performance against fully fine-tuned EEG models and in prospective clinical workflows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Your Vision Foundation Model Is Secretly an EEG Foundation Model

title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models
authors: Zhiqun Zhao, Xiaodong Yang, Bruce Gu, Ming Li, Yi Fu, Song Li
abstract: Benchmark scores for medical large language models (LLMs) are difficult to interpret when scoring criteria cannot be traced to clinical evidence. Here we developed Med Evidence Bench (MEB; https://www.medevidencebench.org.cn/), comprising 1,536 physician-constructed items across three levels: guideline knowledge, standardized clinical scenarios and real-world laboratory scenarios. Each criterion stating a medical claim is linked to a versioned source-text span. Across ten LLMs, the Evidence Trace Score (ETS) was 0.975-0.997 for guideline knowledge, 0.292-0.658 for standardized scenarios and 0.182-0.447 for real-world scenarios, and rankings varied across levels. For real-world scenarios, scores for identifying clinical information (mean, 0.770) exceeded those for matching evidence (0.165) or formulating recommendations (0.160). On 1,296 criterion-level judgments, automated grading agreed with the majority vote of three physicians (macro-F1, 0.930; 95% confidence interval, 0.915-0.945), although agreement was lower for evidence application. These findings from Chinese-language materials indicate that guideline recall does not ensure patient-specific evidence use and do not establish clinical effectiveness.

infographic.key_insight: Strong guideline recall did not translate into patient-specific evidence use across ten medical LLMs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Medical AI evaluation should test evidence application in clinical scenarios, not guideline knowledge alone.
method: Developed Med Evidence Bench with 1,536 physician-constructed items across three levels.
Linked every medical-claim scoring criterion to a versioned source-text span.
Evaluated ten LLMs and compared automated grading with physician judgments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evidence Trace Scores ranged from 0.975–0.997 for guideline knowledge but 0.182–0.447 for real-world scenarios; automated grading achieved macro-F1 0.930 against physician-majority judgments.
infographic.watch_item: Results derive from Chinese-language materials and do not establish clinical effectiveness; grading agreement was lower for evidence application.
infographic.paper_title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models

title: CaseScope: A Multi-Field Benchmark for Case-Level Pathology Diagnosis with Multimodal LLMs
authors: Wenchuan Zhang, Chengyang Zhang, Fengling Li, Ting Yin, Chen Shu, Jie Chen
abstract: Pathologists rarely diagnose from a single image: they scan a section at low power for architecture, zoom into selected fields for cytology, and integrate the evidence across views and scales. Pathology benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), however, mostly ask about one image or require whole-slide pipelines, and the few that show several fields draw nested regions from cancer slides of one public cohort. We introduce CaseScope, a benchmark of diagnosis from several curated fields of one lesion: CaseScope-Teaching, 436 cases from a residency-training image library, reconstructed, de-identified, harmonised against a WHO-based ontology and re-examined by a pathologist wherever an automated pre-review raised a doubt, and CaseScope-Atlas, 800 cases from 88 published atlases (387 of them figure series of one disease), labelled from the captions by two LLMs that must agree. They cover 843 entities across 18 organ systems and pose 4,679 items in six tasks, from open-ended and ten-way diagnosis with ontology-guided hard negatives under circular evaluation to the verification and location of morphological findings. Across twenty-eight open and four proprietary MLLMs, diagnoses are unstable -- the best open and proprietary models are correct under all ten option rotations on 17.9% and 61.7% of the teaching cases -- and wrong answers favour the classic look-alike; open models make little use of the additional fields on teaching cases, where the one-line specimen site matters more, although on atlas cases with three or more fields the fields count about as much as the site; and most open models verify findings barely above chance (median 62.0% vs. 50%, best 81.5%), gaining a median +3.4 points from images; proprietary models reach 83.2-93.2%. Rankings broadly replicate between the sources. The evaluation code is available at https://github.com/Wenchuan-Zhang/CaseScope.

infographic.key_insight: CaseScope exposes unstable case-level pathology diagnosis in multimodal LLMs: the best open and proprietary models answered correctly across all ten option rotations on just 17.9% and 61.7% of teaching cases, respectively.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark tests integration of multiple pathology fields, highlighting reliability gaps relevant to evaluating potential diagnostic support tools.
method: Combined 436 residency-teaching cases with 800 cases from 88 published pathology atlases.
Evaluated six tasks spanning diagnosis, morphological finding verification, and finding localization.
Tested 28 open and four proprietary multimodal LLMs, including sensitivity to answer-option order.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 4,679 items covering 843 entities and 18 organ systems, most open models verified findings only modestly above chance, while model rankings broadly replicated across the two sources.
infographic.watch_item: Curated teaching and atlas fields, including atlas labels derived through agreement between two LLMs, do not establish performance in prospective clinical workflows.
infographic.paper_title: CaseScope: A Multi-Field Benchmark for Case-Level Pathology Diagnosis with Multimodal LLMs

title: Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment
authors: Guoqing Zhang, Rafik Hadfi, Takayuki Ito
abstract: Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission is a critical benchmark for evaluating healthcare quality. Most predictive models assume readmission risk depends solely on a patient's individual pathophysiological state, ignoring hospital operational context and resource capacity. In practice, discharge decisions are dynamic trade-offs between patient stability and bed turnover pressures. To address this gap, we develop an Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for ICU discharge risk assessment. The system combines multi-agent collaborative extraction with self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate template noise from progress notes, while constructing departmental workload indicators alongside admission flow features, continuous vital signs, and sparse medical codes (ICD/DRG). Addressing severe class imbalance (about 10.5% readmissions) and alarm fatigue, we implement data normalization, class reweighting, and decision-threshold calibration. In 20 independent runs across 20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical findings demonstrate that: vital signs alone have limited predictive capacity under real-world class imbalance (PR-AUC of 0.1387 +/- 0.0086); directly concatenating raw text embeddings degrades decision tree performance (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030); whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture (Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter freezing and differential learning rates reverses text negative transfer, achieving the highest AUROC of 0.8288 +/- 0.0110, PR-AUC of 0.4373 +/- 0.0310, and F1-Score of 0.4757 +/- 0.0196. Operational indicators supply independent risk signals, laying an engineering foundation for high-utility clinical decision support tools.

infographic.key_insight: An operation-aware multimodal model combining patient data, clinical notes, and hospital workload achieved the strongest ICU readmission prediction among the evaluated approaches.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Incorporating operational context may help discharge-risk tools reflect both patient condition and hospital pressures, but clinical benefit remains unproven.
method: Combined workload and admission-flow indicators with vital signs, ICD/DRG codes, and clinical notes.
Used multi-agent extraction and self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation to remove note-template noise.
Applied end-to-end Transformer fine-tuning, class reweighting, and decision-threshold calibration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 20 independent runs on 20,000 MIMIC-III ICU stays with approximately 10.5% readmissions, the best model achieved AUROC 0.8288 ± 0.0110, PR-AUC 0.4373 ± 0.0310, and F1 0.4757 ± 0.0196.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no external or prospective validation; performance and alert burden in other hospitals remain uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment

title: Domain adaptation of a video Foundation model for Heart Failure Diagnosis from Echocardiography
authors: Mahyar Bolhassani, Tijana Geroski, Narayana S. Singam, Amir Amini
abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models has transformed computer vision, yet their adaptation to medical imaging, particularly purpose built foundation models for spatio temporal echocardiography videos, remains limited. In this work, we explore the feasibility of fine tuning a pretrained foundation model for video (TimeSformer) for automated diagnosis of reduced ejection fraction heart failure (HFrEF) from apical four chamber videos. The model is finetuned on the publicly available RVENet A4C dataset with a phase aware clip generation strategy that captures complementary systolic and diastolic dynamics. We employ divided space time attention, layer wise learning rate decay, and multi clip inference to enhance robustness under limited data. Experimental results show that full fine tuning of the proposed model outperforms classifier only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline. These findings highlight the potential of leveraging foundation video models for echocardiography based heart failure diagnosis and motivates further domain adaptation studies in medical imaging.

infographic.key_insight: Fully fine-tuning a pretrained TimeSformer video model outperformed classifier-only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline for identifying HFrEF from echocardiography videos.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Video foundation models could support echocardiography-based HFrEF assessment, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Fine-tuned TimeSformer on apical four-chamber videos from the public RVENet A4C dataset.
Generated phase-aware clips capturing complementary systolic and diastolic dynamics.
Used divided space-time attention, layer-wise learning rate decay, and multi-clip inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on RVENet A4C favored full fine-tuning over classifier-only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline; the abstract reports no numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: External validation is not described in the abstract, leaving generalizability across clinical settings uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Domain adaptation of a video Foundation model for Heart Failure Diagnosis from Echocardiography
